pages.title: JBPA Management Platform
pages.subtitle: High-Level Architecture | Customer-deployable Private Agent lifecycle management
intro: This build is a reusable management product that customers deploy in their own environment. It exposes supported JBPA actions through Jitterbit MCP, delivers requests through API Manager, Studio and JBMQ, and executes them from a dedicated Linux management host against explicitly named target VMs.

The management host runs a REST API, a background worker, PostgreSQL and an HTTPS entry point in containers. The existing JBPA caller remains the lifecycle engine. Target hosts use their existing SSH access; no additional listening service is introduced on the PA hosts.
cards: Versioned containers, configuration contracts, job APIs and a matching Jitterbit project kit.
Accept and identify the job, queue delivery, execute through SSH, retain the validated result.
A standard install/upgrade/recovery experience across permitted hosts and independent customer deployments.
pages.callout: Proposed product architecture. The management stack is not yet implemented or production-qualified; scoped JBPA evidence and release gates are documented in the qualification section.

sections.title: Architecture views
sections.text: The deployment view locates concrete services, interfaces and trust zones. Admission connects request validation to atomic persistence and queue publication. The execution protocol separates queue acknowledgement from SSH work. Data ownership, target resolution, recovery and result projection each have a dedicated technical view.

sections.title: Evidence boundary
sections.text: All diagrams describe the proposed product design. Existing JBPA lifecycle evidence is scoped to documented OS/package combinations. Product implementation and qualification remain release gates; they are not inferred from this architecture document.

pages.title: Purpose, outcomes and design boundaries
pages.subtitle: The design connects customer deployment, agent management and operational accountability.
intro: Installations may take several minutes and may restart or remove the target agent. The component initiating the change must therefore remain available independently of that target. The first AI/API call returns durable acceptance and a job ID; execution and result retrieval continue independently of the conversation.

Each customer operates a separate deployment of the same product release. Customer-specific inventory, credentials, certificates, access policy and Harmony configuration are external to the image. The product starts after target infrastructure has been provisioned.

sections.title: Non-negotiable boundaries
sections.text: No arbitrary host or shell command is accepted from an AI request. Install does not silently become upgrade or reinstall. Local uninstall does not delete Harmony records. A timeout does not prove the remote action failed. Supported OS/package tuples, upgrade edges and artifact provenance govern production execution.

pages.title: Deployment topology and trust zones
pages.subtitle: Actual components, private ports, credential placement and target-host separation.
pages.caption: Jitterbit owns the tool/API facade and queue delivery. The dedicated management host exposes only HTTPS; API and database ports are internal. Worker requests use pinned SSH access to named target VMs. Responses use the same connections.

sections.text: Any eligible management PA may dispatch the request to the same parent endpoint. The dedicated parent resolves the requested target. A target PA can be offline or absent and still be managed over SSH. [J2]

pages.callout: Jitterbit is the licensed integration layer. Open-source management components reduce custom infrastructure code; they do not make the entire solution license-free.

pages.title: API technology - reuse the Python investment
pages.subtitle: FastAPI defines the contract; the separate worker owns long-running execution.

blocks.title: Python + existing JBPA
blocks.text:
WHY: the repository already contains lifecycle adapters, release validation and a structured SSH caller.
VALUE: wrapping the fixed caller preserves its checks instead of duplicating install logic.
REUSE: API and worker share request/result models and one application image. Other clients can use the same REST API.
TRADEOFF: remote attempt recovery and a production execution profile still require code changes.

blocks.title: FastAPI + Pydantic
blocks.text:
WHY: typed request/response models support validation and OpenAPI/JSON Schema generation. [T1, T2]
VALUE: reject invalid target/action/version input early and keep Jitterbit transformations aligned with the API.
REUSE: model definitions become documentation, tests and client schemas.
TRADEOFF: validation is not authorization; action/target checks remain application responsibilities.

blocks.title: Uvicorn + separate worker
blocks.text:
WHY: Uvicorn serves the ASGI API; a separate process claims durable READY jobs.
VALUE: API restarts do not erase accepted execution work.
REUSE: the same worker image can run with different permitted inventories.
TRADEOFF: process restart does not prove a remote mutation stopped; reconcile its original attempt.

blocks.title: Alternatives considered
blocks.text: Flask can serve this API but needs more explicit schema integration. Node.js/Go would introduce another language around a Python execution engine. FastAPI in-memory background tasks are insufficient as the durable job mechanism. A new Celery/Redis stack is not required for the initial product.

pages.title: Database technology - durability and coordination
pages.subtitle: PostgreSQL is selected for the product baseline, including customers with more than one worker.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL
blocks.text:
WHY: transactional creation of job + outbox, uniqueness for idempotency, and controlled concurrent claims. [T3]
VALUE: results and ownership survive application restarts; uncertain actions remain visible.
REUSE: customers can use the bundled DB or a qualified external PostgreSQL service.
TRADEOFF: backups, migrations and restoration are required operations.

blocks.title: Worker ownership
blocks.text:
WHY: a queue can redeliver and a worker can fail mid-installation.
VALUE: canonical-host ownership prevents simultaneous lifecycle changes across aliases and workers.
REUSE: the same contract works for one worker or a qualified expanded deployment.
TRADEOFF: lease expiry is only a warning; it never independently authorizes replay.

blocks.title: SQLAlchemy + Alembic
blocks.text:
WHY: explicit transactions and schema changes tracked as released migrations.
VALUE: every customer can upgrade through a tested version sequence.
REUSE: application repositories, migration tests and database compatibility checks are shared product code.
TRADEOFF: migrations must be reviewed and run once; database portability is not promised merely by using an ORM.

blocks.title: Why not SQLite or another broker?
blocks.text: SQLite fits a small local tool, but PostgreSQL is the deliberate shared-service baseline for this product. JBMQ already handles external delivery; the parent database holds accepted worker jobs. A second broker would add deployment and recovery responsibilities without a demonstrated requirement.

pages.title: Packaging technology - portable and replaceable
pages.subtitle: The deployment framework reduces customer setup; it does not replace operational ownership.

blocks.title: Docker Engine + Compose
blocks.text:
WHY: the service topology is bounded and customers requested Linux containers.
VALUE: pinned images, service networks, health checks and persistent volumes make installation reproducible.
REUSE: the same release runs in each qualified customer environment.
TRADEOFF: Compose is a single-host baseline; Docker Desktop and Kubernetes are not prerequisites. [T4, L9-L11]

blocks.title: NGINX Open Source
blocks.text:
WHY: provide a standard TLS entry point separately from application code.
VALUE: centralize certificates, request limits and proxy routing; keep API/DB ports internal.
REUSE: customers may substitute their existing qualified gateway without changing the API.
TRADEOFF: certificate lifecycle and trusted proxy headers need explicit configuration. [L8]

blocks.title: OpenSSH + the existing caller
blocks.text:
WHY: the target already has an established remote administration interface.
VALUE: encrypted access and pinned host identity without adding a PA-host web service.
REUSE: the worker delegates to the existing inventory-based caller rather than building a new transport.
TRADEOFF: credentials, sudo access and interrupted-command evidence must be governed. [L12]

blocks.title: Keep the default deployment bounded
blocks.text: Kubernetes introduces a control plane and operational skills that the first customer package does not require. Managed PostgreSQL and existing reverse proxies are optional integration profiles. Redis/Celery remain unnecessary until a specific worker capability cannot be satisfied by the durable job contract.

pages.title: Fleet targeting and execution isolation
pages.subtitle: Management PA scheduling is independent of the selected lifecycle target.
pages.caption: Both management PAs call one central service. The worker resolves the recorded inventory revision to a canonical host and enforces one active mutation for that host. Aliases cannot bypass ownership, and accepted jobs cannot silently move to another host.

sections.title: Ports and reachability
sections.text: Only the HTTPS entry point is host-published. API :8080 and PostgreSQL :5432 are proposed internal defaults. Management PAs reach the same private parent endpoint. Workers reach target SSH; targets require approved outbound package/download/Harmony access. Backups are retained off-host.

pages.title: Admission, durability and publication
pages.subtitle: The business request becomes a durable job before any queue reference is published.
pages.caption: Parent receipt precedes publication in this recovery-relay view. Submit may publish on its fast path; the job and outbox are committed first. The relay repairs interrupted sends. Reused keys return the original job; changed input with the same key conflicts.

pages.subtitle: Short operations provide the submission, delivery and status facade.

sections.title: Why APIM and Studio add value in this design
sections.text: APIM exposes the supported contract; Studio carries credentials, mappings and queue orchestration. Management PAs bridge the customer network to the private parent endpoint. JBMQ makes delivery asynchronous. A forwarding-only project would add little value, but the queue/relay/status project has a defined role. [J1-J3]

pages.callout: Every management PA uses the same parent URL. Harmony routing selects an execution agent, while the parent inventory selects the lifecycle target.

pages.title: Queue dispatch and durable acknowledgement
pages.subtitle: Delivery acceptance is a short transaction; the installation runs independently.
pages.caption: The dispatcher validates a queue reference and asks the parent to commit READY. A repeated reference returns compatible prior acceptance. Only then does Studio acknowledge the message. Delivery failures receive bounded retry or quarantine; a known installation failure belongs to the job result.

pages.title: Remote execution and host ownership
pages.subtitle: A background worker runs the fixed JBPA caller against the explicitly named target.
pages.caption: The worker claims the job and canonical host, records an attempt and executes through pinned SSH access. The original attempt must remain discoverable after interruption. A resolved result is persisted; an uncertain outcome enters NEEDS_RECONCILIATION with ownership retained. Queue acknowledgements and HTTP calls do not span the installation.

pages.title: Job model and ownership relationships
pages.subtitle: The persistent schema explains what is authoritative and how duplicate or competing work is controlled.
pages.caption: The API creates job and outbox together. Worker claims coordinate through canonical-host ownership; events and evidence remain associated with the same job and attempt. Fields shown are a proposed contract, not an implemented database migration.

pages.title: Recovery and reconciliation decisions
pages.subtitle: Interruption is resolved through original evidence before another mutation can begin.
pages.caption: A transport timeout does not prove that execution stopped or the target remained unchanged. Unknown outcomes keep the host fenced. Only observed evidence can resolve the original action; any subsequent mutation has its own authorization.

pages.title: Result retrieval and response boundary
pages.subtitle: The status call reads the retained job and projects a permitted, sanitized response.
pages.caption: Authorization applies to the job, caller/deployment and target scope. Running jobs remain retrievable; unknown IDs are not guessed to be queued. The client receives a normalized result without credentials or unrestricted vendor logs.

pages.title: Acceptance and delivery guarantees
pages.subtitle: These rules connect the sequence diagrams to the durable job contract.

sections.title: Lost response handling
sections.text: The client may lose a response after the database commits. It retries with the same request identity. The job may already be queued or running, so a fresh identity must not be substituted merely because the initial HTTP call failed.

sections.title: Failure classification
sections.text: Transient delivery problems receive bounded delayed retries. Invalid, unauthorized or inconsistent references go to delivery quarantine/dead-letter review. A known installation failure is a valid business result, not a delivery failure.

pages.callout: The original MCP request returns after durable acceptance. Queue acknowledgements and remote execution outcomes are different facts. Neither a lost HTTP response nor an expired worker lease justifies replaying a mutation.

sections.title: Execution lifecycle
sections.text: ACCEPTED_PENDING_DISPATCH -> READY -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDED or FAILED. An uncertain remote outcome enters NEEDS_RECONCILIATION while host ownership is retained. Queue publication is recorded separately and cannot regress a running or completed job.

sections.title: Idempotency and results
sections.text: Same key + same canonical request returns the same job. Same key + changed parameters is a conflict. Diagnostic status does not prove identity-aware Harmony health. Requested/resolved versions, artifact digest, worker release and attempt identity support reproducible diagnosis.

pages.title: Queue reliability and publication recovery
pages.subtitle: The request queue buffers delivery; the parent database preserves the business record.

rows: Job commit succeeds; queue send fails
Keep outbox entry; relay republishes later

Messages age or queue reaches capacity

sections.title: Acknowledgement and retry
sections.text: ACK only after the parent commits READY or confirms compatible prior acceptance. Use bounded delayed retry. Do not wait for installation before ACK. The queue design must respect the customer tier and avoid assuming additional retry queues are licensed. [J1, J4]

sections.title: Service constraints
sections.text: JBMQ documents a 30-minute acknowledgement timeout and a maximum message TTL of 10 days. Monitor backlog and oldest job; PostgreSQL is the historical source. New submissions require the parent and DB because durable job creation precedes queue publication. [J1]

sections.title: Tool configuration
sections.text: Use the provided Jitterbit MCP server editor: name/description, REST method/endpoint/path, request/response schemas and backend authentication. Resources provide prerequisites/support information; templates provide guided workflows. Production behavior must be validated in the actual tenant.

sections.title: Client-visible contract
sections.text: Return 202 only after durable acceptance, 200 for retrieved results, a stable job ID and honest current state. Expose equivalent errors through APIM: invalid input, unauthenticated, forbidden, not found, conflict and dependency unavailable. Response body alone must never imply installation success.

blocks.title: Error and state semantics
blocks.text:
400/422 invalid input; 401 unauthenticated; 403 forbidden; 404 unknown/not-visible job; 409 conflicting identity/request; 503 dependency unavailable.

READY means accepted for execution. RUNNING means an attempt exists. NEEDS_RECONCILIATION means the original remote outcome must be inspected. Samples are proposed, not observed output.

sections.title: Identity is enforced in the service
sections.text: A shared integration identity receives only its explicit scope. Delegated user identity must be verified, not trusted from model-generated headers. Separate submit, relay, dispatch, read and administrative permissions. Rotate access tokens, TLS and SSH material through tested procedures.

sections.title: Container and evidence isolation
sections.text: No privileged containers or Docker socket mounts. Only HTTPS is published on the management host; API/DB stay internal. Compose secret mounts are protected files, not encryption or a vault. Logs/results are allowlisted and redacted; detailed vendor evidence is restricted.

sections.title: Versions and action boundaries
sections.text: Pin a qualified package/digest and caller release. Do not silently turn install into upgrade/reinstall. Complete local uninstall leaves Harmony record management separate. Mutable latest and unsupported tuples are rejected unless a separately governed qualification mode explicitly permits them.

sections.title: Mapping revisions
sections.text: A job records the inventory revision used at acceptance. If a target mapping changes, execute against the approved recorded mapping or reject/reconcile the job. Never redirect a queued job to a new host silently. [R2-R4]

pages.title: Recover safely when execution is interrupted
pages.subtitle: A timeout means the outcome may be unknown; it does not mean the target is unchanged.

rows: Establish non-start from attempt evidence before resuming
Retain host ownership; inspect original attempt/process/result
Fence abandoned attempt; do not launch a second mutation solely on lease expiry
Preserve safe local/remote evidence and reconcile before new work
Stop dispatch; restore; fence workers; reconcile active jobs and stale queue references
Serve structured failure; new lifecycle action requires its own authorization

sections.title: Required adapter improvement
sections.text: Before any mutation, bind a stable job/attempt identity to the remote command and evidence path. The current synchronous caller discovers some evidence after execution; the product must make interrupted attempts discoverable through SSH without adding a target daemon or port.

sections.title: Execution guarantee
sections.text: Delivery is at least once and requests are idempotent. Exactly-once remote mutation is not claimed. Safety is provided by canonical-host coordination, remote locking, stable evidence and reconciliation. Generic executing-job cancellation and package rollback are excluded until qualified.

sections.title: Package contents
sections.text: Pinned API/worker images; Compose manifests; configuration schemas; database migrations; backup/restore and upgrade tools; target-access validator; version/support matrix; Jitterbit project kit; smoke tests and operator runbooks.

sections.title: Deployment automation limits
sections.text: Container portability does not imply every Linux host is supported. Publish tested distribution/architecture/runtime versions. Use actual Harmony export/import interfaces; retain explicit manual setup steps where automation is not available. A clean-host deployment must pass before claiming easy repeatable installation.

sections.title: Release ownership
sections.text: Keep customer secrets out of images, manifests and queue messages. Publish dependency/runtime support windows and security update guidance. An image rollback is safe only when schema and active-job compatibility are proven.

sections.title: Recovery objectives
sections.text: Agree recovery point/time objectives with each deployment and measure restore drills. A backup file is not proof of successful restoration. Use PostgreSQL-supported backup mechanisms; a future managed DB profile can share the same API/worker contract. [T5]

pages.title: Operate the service and scale deliberately
pages.subtitle: A recoverable single-host baseline supports the first product release; availability claims require evidence.

rows: Review policy, release and access decisions

sections.title: Capacity and availability
sections.text: Benchmark concurrency against target download/installation times, SSH load and DB persistence. Configure bounded worker limits; one mutation per host remains mandatory. Compose restarts processes but cannot survive host loss without recovery. HA requires redundant application hosts, HA PostgreSQL, shared evidence and proven fencing.

sections.title: Support model
sections.text: Product engineering owns released code and compatibility evidence. Customer operations owns hosting, backups and routes. Harmony administrators own queues/projects/licensing. Identity administrators own credential policy. Recovery operators own documented reconciliation decisions.

sections.title: Open-source components versus our own code
sections.text: The API design is reusable through HTTP/OpenAPI and the packaged runtime can be self-hosted. No repository LICENSE file was identified in the current JBPA checkout. Publishing our own code as open source therefore requires an explicit license/ownership decision. Jitterbit binaries, branding, credentials and vendor artifacts are not automatically covered by upstream component licenses.

sections.title: Docker licensing boundary
sections.text: The deployment uses Linux Docker Engine and Compose. Docker Desktop is a separate product with subscription terms; it is not a customer runtime prerequisite. Registry access, support, host infrastructure and Jitterbit licensing remain costs to assess. [L9-L11]
